In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

abstract concepts, which refer to intangible elements of experience, such as internal states, emotions, and social activities, are represented in the human brain by neural patterns that represent the specific components of semantic content that are central to each concept.
this study provides evidence for the neural basis of semantic representations of abstract conceptual content.
abstract concepts, in addition to concrete concepts, activate distributed neural representations of semantic content.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the meaning of abstract concepts is grounded in nonlinguistic conceptual content.
the meanings of both concrete and abstract concepts rest on neural patterns supporting internal representations of how to interact with entities in the world, and with other people.

the meaning of abstract concepts is grounded in nonlinguistic conceptual knowledge, and that the meaning of concrete concepts is grounded in the sensorimotor systems that underlie perception of the physical objects and actions to which the concepts refer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, rather than occurring in a single brain region and/or across-all-brain regions uniformly, neural representations of concepts are distributed across specific sets of brain regions.
the neural representations of abstract concepts mimic the rich content of concrete concepts, rather than abstract concepts being represented as thin or sparse entities.
, like concrete entities, abstract concepts appear to elicit patterns of distributed neural activity that reflect the semantic content of abstract ideas.
